author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Origen offers brief explanatory notes on selected verses of Genesis, addressing textual difficulties, moral and theological questions, and apparent contradictions for readers of the Greek Bible.
argument: Origen explains that the flood was not an act of divine anger or regret but a deliberate change in God's providential plan to destroy Cain's line while preserving the righteous Noah. He interprets the fire that destroyed Sodom as a sign of the coming consummation, and connects Lot's wife becoming a pillar of salt to a spiritual warning about losing one's saltiness. He notes that the four hundred didrachms paid for Abraham's burial field are significant because the numbers four and one hundred are harmful. He asks whether Joseph's dream about his mother and brothers bowing to him may prophesy Mary and Joseph worshiping Christ. Finally, he suggests that Joseph's steward seems to have benefited in piety from Joseph, and explains why the Hebrews' identity as shepherds made them an abomination to the Egyptians.

outline.move: Explains why God sent the flood, why animals were included, why clean animals were taken by sevens—three pairs for breeding and one for sacrifice, since God was about to permit meat-eating and sacrifices—and how God's 'repentance' means a change in his providential plan.
Interprets the fire that destroyed Sodom as a sign of the coming consummation, and connects Lot's wife becoming a pillar of salt to the sayings about salt losing its savor.
Notes that the four hundred didrachms paid for the burial field are significant because the numbers four and one hundred are harmful.
Observes that Joseph's mother had died before his dreams and asks whether the dream may prophesy Mary and Joseph worshiping Christ.
Suggests that Joseph's steward seems to have benefited in piety from his time with Joseph.
Explains why the Hebrews' identity as shepherds made them an abomination to the Egyptians.

key_terms.sense: God's 'repentance' or change of plan, understood not as human regret but as a shift in divine providence.
God's ordered management or providential arrangement of events.
Ritually clean animals, fit for sacrifice and food.
Ritually unclean animals, not fit for sacrifice.
The pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was turned, interpreted as a spiritual warning.
The final consummation or end of the age, prefigured by the fire that destroyed Sodom.
The four hundred didrachms paid for the burial field, whose numbers are harmful.
Something ritually detestable or abominable to the Egyptians.
A shepherd of sheep, an occupation abhorrent to Egyptians but honorable for Hebrews.

scripture: Origen cites the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint). Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint. Book names should be given in modern English form (e.g., Genesis, Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel).
uncertain: The exact date of composition beyond 'early 3rd century'.
Whether the work was originally a continuous commentary or a collection of scholia.
The precise identity of the 'some' whose view on divine anger Origen rejects.
